## Simple explanation

Classification predicts a category for an input, such as identifying the
objects in an image or deciding whether a message is spam.

## Technical explanation

A classification model maps features to class scores or probabilities.
Tasks may be binary, multiclass, or multilabel. Training usually uses
labeled examples and a loss function; predictions may use an argmax rule
or application-specific thresholds.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Classification is used for routing, detection, moderation, diagnosis
support, and many other tasks. Class imbalance, differing error costs,
calibration, and changing input distributions all affect how a classifier
should be evaluated and deployed.

## How it works

The model learns a mapping from input features to target labels using a
training objective. At inference, it produces class scores and a decision
rule converts those scores into labels. Evaluation compares predictions
with held-out labeled examples using suitable metrics.

## Practical example

A photo classifier can assign each image to one of two classes, penguin
or ostrich. The accompanying [fast.ai notebook](../../notebooks/B/binary-classification.ipynb)
scaffolds this beginner-friendly binary classification task.

## Common misconceptions

- Classification predicts discrete labels; regression predicts continuous
  values, though some systems combine both.
- A class score is not necessarily a calibrated probability.
- Accuracy alone may hide poor performance on rare classes.
